description: Run a script on Linux instance to perform memory load investigation

s3Location.description: S3 location to load the results into bucket

AccessKeyId.description: (Required) AccesskeyID to store evidence details in S3.

SecretAccessKey.description: (Required) SecretAccessKey to store evidence details in S3

SessionToken.description: (Required) SessionToken to store evidence details in S3.

s3Bucket.description: (Required) S3 bucket location of captured memory

runCommand: #!/bin/bash
# Linux memory load investigation. This runs on the Amazon Linux 2023 forensic
# analysis host built by image-builder-components/forensic-analysis-tools.yml,
# never on the instance under investigation.
set -o pipefail
fail() { echo "MEMORY_INVESTIGATION_FAILED: $1" >&2; exit 1; }
# /tmp on Amazon Linux 2023 is a RAM backed tmpfs capped at half of memory, so
# on the m4.2xlarge analysis host it holds only ~16 GiB and every page written
# there is a page volatility3 and the plaso container cannot use. Peak usage
# below is the compressed capture plus the decompressed image, because gzip -d
# only unlinks its source once it has succeeded: about 2.7x the target's memory
# size, which overflows tmpfs for every target from m5.xlarge upwards.
# createForensicInstance user data mounts a dedicated 512 GiB EBS volume at
# /data, so do all of the large work there.
work_root=/data/forensic-analysis
# Evidence paths are per instance, so an unresolved instance id makes two
# investigations overwrite each other. The old expression used {17\} inside a
# BRE, where the brace is literal, so it never matched anything.
instance=$(printf '%s' '{{s3MemoryCaptureKey}}' | grep -oE 'i-[0-9a-f]{17}' | head -1)
if [ -z "$instance" ]; then
instance=$(printf '%s' '{{s3MemoryCaptureKey}}' | grep -oE 'i-[0-9a-f]{8}' | head -1)
fi
[ -n "$instance" ] || fail 'no instance id in the memory capture key - refusing to write evidence to a shared path'
evidence_dir=$work_root/data/{{forensicID}}_evidence_dir/$instance
working_dir=$work_root/data/{{forensicID}}_working_dir/$instance
# vol.py writes here first. working_dir is uploaded to S3 wholesale, so a
# plugin that fails must not be able to leave a file behind in it.
scratch_dir=$work_root/scratch/{{forensicID}}/$instance
# Pinned so an incident does not pick up whatever the default branch is
# that day. v2.28.0 is the oldest release that walks tasks on Linux 6.12+.
VOL3_REF=v2.28.0
tools_dir=$work_root/tools

mkdir -p "$evidence_dir" "$working_dir" "$scratch_dir" "$tools_dir" 2>/dev/null || { sudo mkdir -p "$evidence_dir" "$working_dir" "$scratch_dir" "$tools_dir" && sudo chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" "$work_root"; } || fail "cannot create the work area under $work_root"
# The whole point of working under /data is that it is not RAM. If the EBS
# volume never got mounted, say so instead of quietly filling memory.
fs_type=$(stat -f -c %T "$work_root" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
case "$fs_type" in
tmpfs|ramfs) fail "$work_root is on a RAM backed $fs_type - decompressing the capture there would exhaust memory. Expected the EBS volume mounted at /data." ;;
esac
# Why AWS credentials arrive as document parameters rather than an instance role:
# these are short-lived STS session credentials, minted per acquisition by the
# forensic Lambda with a session policy scoped to this case's S3 prefix - not
# long-lived IAM access keys. The host this runs on cannot be given an instance
# profile for the evidence bucket: it is either the machine under investigation,
# whose configuration must not be changed mid-incident, or an analysis host that
# must not hold standing access to other cases' evidence. Do not copy this
# pattern into a workload where an IAM role is available.
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID={{AccessKeyId}}
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY={{SecretAccessKey}}
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN={{SessionToken}}
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION={{Region}}
sudo yum update -y
# Volatility 3 requires Python 3.8 or newer (REQUIRED_PYTHON_VERSION in
# volatility3/framework/constants) and upstream only tests installs against
# 3.10 to 3.13, so provision one of those from the distribution package manager.
# Python 3.9 went end of life in October 2025, so compiling 3.9.16 from source
# here left an interpreter that no package manager patched for CVEs.
# /usr/bin/python3 is deliberately NOT repointed: apt and dnf are written against
# the system interpreter, so replacing it breaks package management on the host.
apt_refreshed=0
install_interpreter() {
if command -v apt-get >/dev/null 2>&1; then
if [ "$apt_refreshed" -eq 0 ]; then
sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y update >/dev/null 2>&1
apt_refreshed=1
fi
sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y install "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1
elif command -v dnf >/dev/null 2>&1; then
sudo dnf install -y -q "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1
elif command -v yum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
sudo yum install -y -q "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1
fi
PY=
for candidate in python3.13 python3.12 python3.11 python3.10; do
command -v "$candidate" >/dev/null 2>&1 || install_interpreter "$candidate"
if command -v "$candidate" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
PY=$candidate
break
fi
done
if [ -z "$PY" ]; then
# No supported interpreter is packaged for this analysis host (Ubuntu 20.04
# stops at 3.9, for example). Fall back to the system interpreter only while it
# still clears volatility3's own 3.8 floor, and say so loudly.
if python3 -c 'import sys; sys.exit(0 if sys.version_info >= (3, 8) else 1)' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
PY=python3
echo "WARNING: no supported python3.10 or newer interpreter is available from the package manager, falling back to end-of-life $(python3 --version 2>&1)" >&2
else
fail "no python interpreter meeting volatility3's minimum of 3.8 is available on this analysis host"
fi
fi
echo "using python interpreter $PY ($($PY --version 2>&1))"
cd "$evidence_dir" || fail "cannot enter $evidence_dir"
aws configure set default.s3.max_concurrent_requests 100
{{s3DownloadCommands}} || fail 'downloading the memory capture from S3 failed'
ls -lar >&2
capture_gz=$evidence_dir/linux_memcapture.lime.gz
capture=$evidence_dir/linux_memcapture.lime
test -s "$capture_gz" || fail 'the downloaded memory capture is missing or empty'
aws s3api head-object --bucket '{{s3Bucket}}' --key '{{s3MemoryCaptureKey}}/linux_memcapture.lime.gz' > s3HeadResponse.json || fail 'cannot read the memory capture metadata from S3'
# Free space is reported for the record but not gated on. A guess at the
# compression ratio cuts both ways: at 4x the archive it refused captures
# that would have fitted (a 256 GiB target compressing 2:1 needs 256 GiB but
# was asked for 512 GiB), and a mostly-zero-page capture compresses far
# better than 4x and passed the check before hitting ENOSPC anyway. The
# gzip -d below is checked, which is what actually catches a short volume.
gz_bytes=$(stat -c %s "$capture_gz")
avail_bytes=$(df -Pk "$evidence_dir" | awk 'NR==2 {printf "%.0f", $4 * 1024}')
echo "decompressing ${gz_bytes} compressed bytes into ${work_root}, ${avail_bytes:-unknown} bytes free"
# -f so a retry of this document on the same analysis host overwrites the
# image a previous attempt already expanded. Without it gzip refuses with
# 'already exists' and the fail above turns a resumable retry into a dead end.
gzip -d -f "$capture_gz" || fail 'decompressing the memory capture failed - check for ENOSPC on the work volume'
# A capture can be the right size and still contain nothing. Verified live: a
# LiME acquisition on a freshly booted t3.small produced a 2.08 GiB image that
# was 98.9% zero bytes with no kernel banner anywhere in it, so volatility3
# could not identify the kernel and every plugin failed with
# 'Unsatisfied requirement ... kernel.symbol_table_name'. That is a bad
# capture, not a bad symbol table, and the difference matters: the first is
# fixed by re-acquiring, the second by building an ISF. Say which one it is
# instead of reporting four failed plugins.
# Any real Linux memory image contains the banner - it is what volatility3
# matches an ISF against - so this cannot reject a usable capture.
if ! LC_ALL=C grep -a -q -m1 'Linux version ' "$capture"; then
# tr -d '\000' deletes NUL bytes. Written as '\\000' this deleted
# backslashes and the character '0' instead, so a 97.7% NUL capture was
# reported as 2086487539 of 2086711456 bytes non-zero - the opposite of
# the truth, in the one message an operator has to act on.
nonzero=$(LC_ALL=C tr -d '\000' < "$capture" | wc -c)
total=$(stat -c %s "$capture")

fail "the memory capture contains no kernel banner and is only $nonzero of $total bytes non-zero - the acquisition tool did not read the target's memory. Check acquisition-tool in the capture's S3 metadata for which one ran, then re-acquire; no symbol table can make this capture analysable."
fi
test -s "$capture" || fail 'the decompressed memory capture is missing or empty'
ls -lar >&2
jq '.Metadata' s3HeadResponse.json > s3meta.json || fail 'cannot parse the memory capture metadata'
kernel_name=$(jq -r '.["kernel-name"] // empty' s3meta.json)
kernel_version=$(jq -r '.["kernel-release"] // empty' s3meta.json)
# Both values were written by the instance under investigation, where a root
# attacker controls uname and PATH, so on this host they are untrusted input.
# They are only ever used to build a file name: accept nothing but a plain
# kernel token, and never interpolate them into a shell command or into an
# interpreter program text.
validate_kernel_token() {
[ -n "$2" ] || fail "$1 is missing from the memory capture metadata"
[ "$2" != null ] || fail "$1 is null in the memory capture metadata"
[ "${#2}" -le 128 ] || fail "$1 in the memory capture metadata is too long to be a kernel token"
[[ $2 =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9._+-]+$ ]] || fail "$1 in the memory capture metadata is not a plain kernel token - refusing to use it"
validate_kernel_token kernel-name "$kernel_name"
validate_kernel_token kernel-release "$kernel_version"
echo "capture reports kernel $kernel_name-$kernel_version"
# Which tool produced this image, for the examiner reading this log rather than
# the object's metadata. Reported, not trusted: every one of these values was
# written by the host under investigation, using credentials that host held, so
# a root attacker there could have set them. It is provenance to corroborate,
# not proof - which is why it is only ever echoed, never used in a decision.
acquisition_tool=$(jq -r '.["acquisition-tool"] // "unrecorded"' s3meta.json | LC_ALL=C tr -cd '[:alnum:]._+-' | cut -c1-64)
acquisition_tool_version=$(jq -r '.["acquisition-tool-version"] // "unrecorded"' s3meta.json | LC_ALL=C tr -cd '[:alnum:]._+-' | cut -c1-64)
acquisition_tool_origin=$(jq -r '.["acquisition-tool-origin"] // "unrecorded"' s3meta.json | LC_ALL=C tr -cd '[:alnum:]._+-' | cut -c1-64)
acquisition_attempt=$(jq -r '.["acquisition-attempt"] // "unrecorded"' s3meta.json | LC_ALL=C tr -cd '[:alnum:]' | cut -c1-8)

echo "capture reports acquisition by ${acquisition_tool:-unrecorded} ${acquisition_tool_version:-unrecorded} (${acquisition_tool_origin:-unrecorded}) on attempt ${acquisition_attempt:-unrecorded} - as reported by the acquiring host, not independently verified"
cd "$tools_dir" || fail "cannot enter $tools_dir"
# The tools loader uploads to tools/volatility3/, not tools/volatility/.
aws s3 cp s3://{{s3Bucket}}/tools/volatility3/volatility3.zip .
if [ -s volatility3.zip ]; then
# -o, and clear the target first: unzip prompts before overwriting an
# existing tree, reads EOF because SSM gives it no tty, exits 1 and leaves
# the stale copy in place.
rm -rf volatility3
unzip -q -o volatility3.zip || fail 'cannot unpack the staged volatility3 archive'
echo successfully downloaded volatility3 from S3
else
rm -rf volatility3
git clone --branch "$VOL3_REF" --depth 1 https://github.com/volatilityfoundation/volatility3.git || fail "cannot clone volatility3 $VOL3_REF"
echo S3 download not found so downloading from internet
fi
# Volatility 3 releases before 2.28.0 parse a Linux 6.12+ capture without
# error but walk no tasks, so every plugin writes an empty result file and
# the investigation reports success. Refuse to run below that floor.
VOL3_MIN=2.28.0
vol3_detect() {
local v
v=$( (cd volatility3 && PYTHONPATH=. $PY -c 'from volatility3.framework import constants; print(constants.PACKAGE_VERSION)') 2>/dev/null )
if [ -z "$v" ]; then
v=$( (cd volatility3 && $PY vol.py --help 2>&1 | grep -oE 'Volatility 3 Framework [0-9.]+' | head -1 | awk '{print $4}') )
fi
vol3_version=$(vol3_detect)
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$VOL3_MIN" "$vol3_version" | sort -V | head -1)" != "$VOL3_MIN" ]; then
echo "volatility3 $vol3_version is older than $VOL3_MIN - refreshing from upstream" >&2
sudo rm -rf volatility3
git clone --branch "$VOL3_REF" --depth 1 https://github.com/volatilityfoundation/volatility3.git || fail "cannot clone volatility3 $VOL3_REF"
vol3_version=$(vol3_detect)
fi
echo "using volatility3 $vol3_version"
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$VOL3_MIN" "$vol3_version" | sort -V | head -1)" != "$VOL3_MIN" ]; then
fail "volatility3 $vol3_version cannot analyse modern Linux kernels reliably; aborting rather than producing empty evidence"
fi
# --symbol-dirs takes directories, and vol.py prepends them to the built in
# search path, so hand it the symbols directory the ISF was downloaded into.
symbol_dir=$tools_dir/volatility3/volatility3/symbols
symbol_path=$symbol_dir/$kernel_name-$kernel_version.json

aws s3 cp "s3://{{s3ProfileBucket}}/{{s3ProfileLocation}}/$kernel_name-$kernel_version.json" "$symbol_dir/" || fail "no kernel symbol table for $kernel_name-$kernel_version in s3://{{s3ProfileBucket}}/{{s3ProfileLocation}}"
# Quote the operand. With an unquoted [ ! -f $symbol_path ] a value containing
# whitespace makes [ exit 2, which if treats as false, so the guard failed open
# and execution reached the interpreter with no symbol file present at all.
[ -f "$symbol_path" ] || fail "kernel symbol table $kernel_name-$kernel_version.json does not exist on this host"
[ -s "$symbol_path" ] || fail "kernel symbol table $kernel_name-$kernel_version.json is empty"
# Shape is not content: a partial dwarf2json run yields a file of about 134
# bytes whose maps are all empty, which passes an 'is the key present' test and
# then makes every plugin return zero rows. Require populated maps plus what
# volatility3 actually reads: symbols.linux_banner.constant_data, which is the
# only thing automagic can match an ISF to a capture with (see
# framework/automagic/symbol_cache.py), init_task to walk processes, and the
# task_struct definition. The path goes in through argv, never through the
# program text.

$PY -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1])); s=d.get("symbols") or {}; b=d.get("base_types") or {}; u=d.get("user_types") or {}; banner=(s.get("linux_banner") or {}).get("constant_data"); sys.exit(0 if (s and b and u and banner and "init_task" in s and "task_struct" in u) else 1)' "$symbol_path" || fail "kernel symbol table $kernel_name-$kernel_version.json is not a usable volatility3 ISF file - refusing to produce empty evidence"
$PY --version
plugin_failures=0
plugins_ok=0
essential_failures=0
failed_plugins=
run_plugin() {
# $1 = volatility3 plugin, $2 = output file base name, $3 = "essential" when
# the investigation is worthless without it.
# The redirect created the output file before vol.py could fail, so a failed
# plugin left a file behind that was hashed and uploaded as evidence - and
# not even an empty one: vol.py writes its 'Unsatisfied requirement' and
# 'A symbol table requirement was not fulfilled' diagnostics to stdout, so
# the artefact looked like a populated result. Write to scratch outside the
# upload directory and publish only once the plugin has actually succeeded.
local partial="$scratch_dir/$2.txt"
rm -f "$partial"
if ! $PY ./volatility3/vol.py --file="$capture" -s "$symbol_dir" "$1" > "$partial"; then
echo "volatility3 plugin $1 failed - not publishing $2.txt" >&2
rm -f "$partial"
plugin_failures=$((plugin_failures + 1))
failed_plugins="$failed_plugins $1"
[ "${3:-}" = essential ] && essential_failures=$((essential_failures + 1))
return 1
fi
if [ ! -s "$partial" ]; then
echo "volatility3 plugin $1 produced no output - not publishing $2.txt" >&2
rm -f "$partial"
plugin_failures=$((plugin_failures + 1))
failed_plugins="$failed_plugins $1"
[ "${3:-}" = essential ] && essential_failures=$((essential_failures + 1))
return 1
fi
mv "$partial" "$working_dir/$2.txt" || fail "cannot publish $2.txt into the evidence directory"
plugins_ok=$((plugins_ok + 1))
# linux.pslist is essential: it is the process view the whole memory
# investigation exists to produce, and a capture it cannot walk is not analysable.
# The rest are corroborating - psaux and psscan add argv and a scan-based second
# opinion, and linux.bash recovers shell history when it can. linux.bash in
# particular crashes inside volatility3 itself on some kernels: on Amazon Linux
# 2023 kernel 6.18.41 it raises
# "AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'i_size'" walking VMAs with
# a null inode. That is an upstream defect in a corroborating plugin and must not
# void a case whose process list, argv and timeline all succeeded.
run_plugin linux.pslist vol3-output-linux_pslist essential
run_plugin linux.psaux vol3-output-linux_psaux
run_plugin linux.psscan vol3-output-linux_psscan
run_plugin linux.bash vol3-output-linux_bash
cd "$working_dir" || fail "cannot enter $working_dir"
# Hash only artefacts that exist and carry data: sha256sum of a missing file
# writes a zero byte _sha256.txt that is then uploaded as if it were evidence.
shopt -s nullglob
for f in vol3-output-*.txt; do
[ -s "$f" ] || continue
sha256sum "$f" > "${f%.txt}_sha256.txt" || fail "cannot hash $f"
done
shopt -u nullglob
sudo yum install docker -y
sudo systemctl start docker
plaso_failed=0
# Bind /data rather than /tmp: the capture and the multi GB plaso storage file
# both live on the EBS volume now, and a storage file on tmpfs is RAM.
# --user 0:0 because the log2timeline/plaso image runs as a non root user and
# the work area under /data is created root owned 0755 by the steps above. The
# previous revision bound /tmp, which is mode 1777, so the container could write
# there without being asked to; /data is not world writable and plaso fails with
# 'Unable to write to storage file' unless it runs as the owner of the mount.
# The forensic AMI pulls plaso by SHA256 digest and records it at
# /etc/forensic-analysis-plaso-image, then tags it locally as
# log2timeline/plaso:latest so `docker run log2timeline/plaso` resolves to the
# pinned image without a pull. That is deterministic while the pre-pulled image
# is present - but if it is ever absent, the bare reference silently falls back
# to pulling :latest from Docker Hub, which is a different, unreviewed plaso.
# Use the recorded digest and fail loudly instead.
plaso_image=$(cat /etc/forensic-analysis-plaso-image 2>/dev/null)

[ -n "$plaso_image" ] || fail 'no pinned plaso image is recorded at /etc/forensic-analysis-plaso-image - this analysis host was not built from the forensic AMI, and running log2timeline/plaso here would pull an unreviewed :latest from Docker Hub'
sudo docker image inspect "$plaso_image" >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail "the pinned plaso image $plaso_image is recorded but not present on this host"
echo "using pinned plaso image $plaso_image"

if ! sudo docker run --user 0:0 -v /data/:/data "$plaso_image" log2timeline -u --status_view none --partitions all --hashers md5 --hasher_file_size_limit 1073741824 --parser linux --storage-file "$working_dir/timeline.plaso" "$capture"; then
echo 'plaso log2timeline failed - no timeline was produced' >&2
plaso_failed=1
# plaso writes straight into working_dir, which is uploaded wholesale a few
# lines below. Drop a partial storage file rather than publish it as a
# timeline: the per plugin staging above exists for exactly this reason.
rm -f "$working_dir/timeline.plaso"
fi
if [ "$plaso_failed" -eq 0 ] && ! sudo docker run --user 0:0 -v /data/:/data "$plaso_image" psort -o l2tcsv -w "$working_dir/webhist.csv" "$working_dir/timeline.plaso"; then
echo 'plaso psort failed - no csv timeline was produced' >&2
plaso_failed=1
rm -f "$working_dir/webhist.csv"
fi
# Upload whatever was produced before reporting failure, so a partial
# investigation still preserves the evidence it did manage to collect.
aws s3 cp "$working_dir" {{s3Location}} --recursive || fail 'uploading the analysis output to S3 failed'
echo s3 cp complete
ls -ltr
rm -rf "$scratch_dir"
if [ "$plugins_ok" -eq 0 ]; then
fail 'no volatility3 plugin produced output for this capture'
fi
# A plaso failure is reported but does not fail the investigation. plaso is a
# filesystem and log timeliner; against a raw physical memory image it is
# supplementary to volatility3, not the evidence this document exists to
# produce. Letting it veto the run meant a complete, valid memory analysis -
# every plugin succeeded and every artefact uploaded - was reported to the
# state machine as MEMORY_INVESTIGATION_FAILED.
if [ "$plaso_failed" -ne 0 ]; then
echo 'WARNING: plaso produced no timeline for this capture; the volatility3 artefacts are unaffected' >&2
fi
# Only an essential plugin failing voids the investigation. The same reasoning
# as plaso above: this rule used to fail the whole case when any single plugin
# failed, so one upstream volatility3 defect in a corroborating plugin reported
# MEMORY_INVESTIGATION_FAILED for a case that had produced a process list, argv,
# a scan-based process list and a plaso timeline, all uploaded. Measured on a live
# Amazon Linux 2023 6.18.41 capture: linux.bash crashed inside volatility3 and
# three plugins plus plaso succeeded. Which plugins failed is always reported, so
# an examiner knows what is missing rather than having to infer it.
if [ -n "$failed_plugins" ]; then
echo "WARNING: volatility3 plugin(s) failed:$failed_plugins - their artefacts were not published; the remaining $plugins_ok plugin(s) were" >&2
fi
if [ "$essential_failures" -gt 0 ]; then
fail "$essential_failures essential volatility3 plugin(s) failed:$failed_plugins (plaso_failed=$plaso_failed) - the artefacts that were produced have been uploaded"
fi
exit 0;
